slides.title: Modern Concurrency in C++20
slides.prompt: C++20 introduced high-level concurrency constructs: std::jthread (auto-joining thread with stop tokens), semaphores (counting_semaphore), latches (std::latch), and barriers (std::barrier).

slides.title: Auto-Joining Thread Class
slides.prompt: Fill in the C++20 thread class that automatically joins on destruction.

slides.title: std::jthread Cooperative Interruption
slides.prompt: How does std::jthread signal a running thread to interrupt or stop its execution?
options: By passing a std::stop_token parameter to the thread function and invoking request_stop()
By forcefully killing the OS thread handle
By throwing a std::thread_interrupted exception across threads
By automatically setting the thread pointer to nullptr
slides.correctAnswer: By passing a std::stop_token parameter to the thread function and invoking request_stop()

slides.title: std::latch vs std::barrier
slides.prompt: What is a major difference between a std::latch and a std::barrier in C++20?
options: A std::latch is a single-use downward counter, whereas a std::barrier is reusable across multiple phases
std::latch works only across processes, whereas std::barrier works only within threads
std::latch requires mutexes, whereas std::barrier is lock-free
slides.correctAnswer: A std::latch is a single-use downward counter, whereas a std::barrier is reusable across multiple phases

slides.title: std::call_once Purpose
slides.prompt: What does std::call_once guarantee when executed concurrently across multiple threads?
options: The provided callable is executed exactly once, even if called simultaneously from multiple threads
The callable runs once per CPU core
The function runs asynchronously in the background
Execution repeats until it succeeds without throwing an exception
slides.correctAnswer: The provided callable is executed exactly once, even if called simultaneously from multiple threads
